paragraphs.heading: What a sea stack is
paragraphs.text: A stack, or sea stack, is a steep and often vertical column, or group of columns, of rock standing in the sea near a coast. It is a coastal landform made by wave erosion, formed over time by wind and water. The word is also used loosely for isolated, steep-sided islets in the ocean, typically of volcanic origin, which may be called volcanic stacks.

paragraphs.heading: The rock that makes a stack
paragraphs.text: Stacks typically form in sedimentary or volcanic rocks that lie in horizontal beds, particularly on limestone and chalk cliffs. These rocks have medium hardness and compressive strength, which gives them moderate resistance to erosion by the sea. A harder layer on top may act as a protective capstone. Cliffs of weaker material, such as claystone or heavily fractured rock, are prone to slump and wear away too quickly to keep vertical pillars. Harder rocks, granite for one, erode through different structural mechanisms.

paragraphs.heading: From crack to cave to arch
paragraphs.text: A stack forms when a headland is worn away bit by bit by hydraulic action and abrasion. It usually begins when the sea attacks weak points in a cliff face, such as steep joints or small fault zones. Bedding planes are another weakness that the force of the sea exploits. The cracks slowly widen into sea caves. If a cave erodes all the way through a headland, a natural arch is formed.

paragraphs.heading: The arch falls
paragraphs.text: Further erosion, through freeze-thaw action and biological weathering, weakens the roof of the arch. At the same time wave action undercuts its legs. In the end gravity brings the roof down. What remains is a vertical pillar of rock cut off on its own: a stack.

paragraphs.heading: Stacks do not last
paragraphs.text: Waves keep attacking a stack at sea level and undercut it until it collapses, leaving a low stump. The stump then usually becomes a small island of rock, low enough for a high tide to submerge. On geological timescales stacks are temporary landforms. As continued erosion by the sea wears them down, they give a visual record of how the headland has retreated.

paragraphs.heading: Birds, climbers and famous stacks
paragraphs.text: Coastal stacks give seabirds critical nesting sites free of predators, and many are prominent rock climbing destinations. The Old Man of Hoy, a 137-metre stack of Old Red Sandstone in Orkney, Scotland, is famous in the history of sea-stack climbing. The tallest sea stack in the world is Ball's Pyramid in Australia, at 562 metres, formed from a remnant volcanic neck. Dún Briste in Ireland, a 50-metre stack, is said to have severed from Downpatrick Head in 1393. St Michael's Arch in Australia was a stack formed in 1867 when a natural arch collapsed, and it collapsed itself in 1959.
